summary: Tested the independence (Poisson-type) model of witness absence on the Type-I line data: for all primes p≡1 (mod 4) ≤ 2·10⁵ (8,977), the empirical probability that no line t ≤ 63 (K=16), t ≤ 127 (K=32) has a witness is 0.00078 and 0.00022, i.e. 0.40 and 0.41 times the product ∏(1−π_t) of the single-line densities (0.00196, 0.00054). Witness counts have variance 5.92 against 4.93 under independence (positive correlation between lines). For K=64 the model predicts 1.5 absences and 0 are observed. So the independence heuristic overstates the tail of failures at the level of line unions, and a Granville-type sieved correction must produce a factor ≈ 0.4 at this scale; the R(p)-level fit P(R=0 | M) itself was not made (R(p) ≥ 2 throughout the range, so there are no zeros to fit).

summary: The Type-I slice (CONDITIONAL_ES Lemma 1.1, parameter t) gives a concrete witness: first witness t_min for primes p≡1 (mod 4) has median 3 over 39,175 primes ≤ 10⁶, so the typical first witness is found by factoring tp+1 ≈ 3p, an integer of size p. The divisor search 'divisor of tp+1 in class −1 mod t' is therefore a factorisation-type problem at small t, and only the Lenstra/Hales regime (t³ > tp+1, i.e. t ≳ √p) is known to be polynomial. The cost of factoring p-size numbers is what a witness search at small t pays.

summary: Genus-character test on the class structure: R(p) class means over the 96 classes mod 840 with p≡1 mod 4 (p ≤ 10⁵) are explained by the 32 real (order ≤ 2) characters of (Z/840)^* with R² = 0.84 (rank 16 on these classes), against a shuffle-null of 0.16 (95th percentile 0.27). summary: Normalised the same SL₂-type words: M(u)M(t)M(v) ∈ SL₂(ℤ) (det 1) and the transpose/reversal symmetry (t,u,v) ↦ (v,u,t) identifies words in pairs; for 147 primes 5 ≤ p < 2000 ≡ 1 (mod 4) the canonical word count (up to reversal) has median 24, min 0 (p=5), max 50. summary: Rational versus integral census on the ES cubic: using the rational parametrisation (Z2056) with x integer and t = u/v, the integrality condition is v·a | nx(u+v) and u·a | nx(u+v). For p = 13, 17, 29 the box u,v ≤ 60, x ≤ 400 contains 874,591, 872,388 and 865,779 rational parameter points, of which 18, 16 and 22 give integral positive solutions; for p=13 the box u,v ≤ 200, x ≤ 200 gives 22 of the 24 positive ordered integer solutions. Integral points are therefore a density ≈ 2·10⁻⁵ subset of the rational parameter points in this box, so rational points do not in practice produce integral ones.

summary: Analysis of the first lemma: the ES Type-I count is Σ_t Σ_{m≡−1 (t)} 1[m | tp+1] with 4 | m. Expanding 1[m | tp+1] additively gives phases e(a(tp+1)/m), which are linear in p and t, not the inverse-type fractions e(a m̄/n) of the Bettin–Chandee bilinear form (arXiv:1502.00769 abstract: bounds for Σ α_m β_n ν_a e(a m̄/n) with arbitrary coefficients, improving Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec). The BC sums are averaged over moduli, so they give statements over ranges of p, not for the fixed prime p of the ES witness; the reduction to an inverse-type phase would need a change of variables that I did not find.
not_done: No Fourier-analytic bound or numerical test of the phase identity; the change of variables was not attempted in detail.
